items.bodyEn: Hiroshige set his Fujikawa print at the bōbana, the marker where the post town began. A procession passes leading horses under a banner, and villagers kneel in the dust. It shows the shogunate's annual Hassaku gift of horses to the imperial court: every eighth month the animals were sent west from Edo to Kyoto along this road.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Fifty-three Stations (Hōeidō ed.), Fujikawa 'Bōbana no zu'

items.bodyEn: 棒鼻 first meant the tip of a carrying pole, the end of the shaft on a palanquin or baggage litter. By extension it came to name the edge of a post town, the point where the highway entered or left the rows of inns, often marked by a signpost or a mound. Fujikawa's keeper borrows the word.
items.sourceNote: Daijisen and Kōjien, entry 棒鼻 (ぼうばな・ぼうはな)

items.bodyEn: The oldest forms of 向 show a house with a window cut into its wall, and the Shuowen Jiezi defines it as a window opening to the north. A window faces one way, so the character came to mean facing or heading toward something. That sense sits behind this station's 〜向け, made for someone, and 〜向き, suited to someone.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi, entry 向 (北出牖也); standard kanji etymological dictionaries

items.bodyEn: Once you have stepped onto a boat that is pushing off, you cannot climb back onto the shore; it leaves with you aboard. Japanese says 乗りかかった船 for a task you are already committed to and must see through. It pairs naturally with this station's 〜からには: now that you have started, there is no turning back.
